justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a mild upward drift from what I'd assume was the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, likely somewhere around $192–194. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to recent price action, expecting minimal deviation and setting the estimate at $193.50. For the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to $194, reflecting a modest positive drift assumption consistent with a stock or asset in a gradual uptrend, while acknowledging that short-term mean reversion could easily offset any gains. At the one-month horizon, the $195 estimate reflects continued mild optimism but little strong directional conviction — essentially a near-flat real expectation with the passage of time doing most of the "work" in widening uncertainty rather than changing the central outlook meaningfully.

The confidence interval widths were driven primarily by the time-scaling of volatility. At one day, the $186–$201 range (roughly ±4%) reflects normal daily-to-weekly price fluctuation for a moderately volatile asset. By one week, the interval widens to $181–$207 (roughly ±7%), capturing the accumulation of daily variance over five trading sessions. At one month, the $170–$222 range (roughly ±13%) reflects the further compounding of uncertainty, consistent with an annualized volatility somewhere in the 25–35% range. I also factored in some asymmetry risk — the upper and lower bounds are roughly symmetric here, which assumes no strong skew at the time of forecasting.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include macroeconomic surprises such as unexpected central bank decisions, inflation prints, or geopolitical shocks that could gap the asset several percentage points in a single session. At the one-month horizon, an earnings release, major analyst rating change, or sector-wide repricing event could easily breach the stated bounds. Liquidity conditions and broader market sentiment shifts — particularly a sudden risk-off move — represent tail risks on the downside that my symmetric intervals may underweight.

On the upside, a short squeeze, unexpected positive news catalyst, or broader market rally driven by positive macro data could push the asset above $222 within a month. The intervals I provided are statistically reasonable under normal market conditions, but financial markets are fat-tailed, meaning true extreme outcomes occur more frequently than a normal distribution would suggest. Anyone relying on these intervals should treat the bounds as approximate guides rather than hard limits, and recognize that roughly 10% of outcomes — by construction — are expected to fall outside them even if the model is perfectly calibrated.
